sources.title: Library of Congress, Mass Deacidification
sources.text:
Some documents are highly susceptible to embrittlement, which can make those documents unusable. Some documents that have acidic paper are susceptible to turning brittle and unusable over time. The chemistry of this is complex, and acid components may come from fiber stock (such as ground wood pulp) or additives (such as bleach or alum rosin size). Once paper is weakened, though, little can be done to restore its original usability.
Good preservation practice is to prevent this decay before papers become fragile. Research has shown that adding alkaline compounds to acidic paper (in a process called deacidification) before embrittlement begins, can extend the life expectancy of these papers.
A successful mass deacidification process must raise pH to 6.8–10.4, achieve at least 1.5% alkaline reserve, and extend useful life by over 300% by fold endurance after accelerated aging.

sources.title: Canadian Conservation Institute, Basic care – Books
sources.locator: Foxing lines 73–76; iron gall ink lines 74–76
sources.text:
On old paper, you may notice reddish-brown or brown spots (called foxing). This is common if paper is stored for long periods in humid conditions. Foxing is thought to be caused by mould. Consult a conservator about what to do.
During the 19th century, iron gall ink was common. It contains acid. When books with iron gall ink are stored in humid conditions, the acid in the ink attacks the paper, creating holes where words were printed.

sources.title: Canadian Conservation Institute, Caring for paper objects
sources.locator: Iron gall ink, lines 142–149; water, lines 260–272; mould and RH, lines 486–530
sources.text:
Iron gall ink is made from gallnut extract, iron sulfate, gum arabic and water. Gallnuts provide gallic and tannic acids that react with iron salts in oxygen to form the ink colourant, initially blue-black and shifting toward brown with age. Iron gall ink can cause ink corrosion and paper degradation. Iron(II) ions and acids may migrate from the ink into surrounding paper in moisture or high relative humidity, increasing corrosion. Affected areas may show cracks and losses at ink lines.
Water exposure can cause loss or bleeding of media, water stains, cockling and surface deformations, delaminations and mould growth. A badly degraded acidic wood-pulp paper absorbs more water, resulting in heavier water staining and tide lines.
Mould may digest paper and produce coloured by-products causing irreversible stains; mould growth can weaken and stain paper. Damp conditions lead to cockling; at very high RH, ink dyes and watercolours risk bleeding.

sources.title: Canadian Conservation Institute, Agent of Deterioration: Water
sources.text: A badly degraded, acidic wood pulp paper will absorb more water, leading to heavier water staining and “tide lines.” Water damage to paper includes softening, running inks, staining, tide lines, distortion (cockling).

sources.title: National Park Service, Conserve O Gram 3/4: Mold: Prevention of Growth in Museum Collections
sources.text: Mold can permanently damage materials supporting it and make them more susceptible to future mold contamination. It can stain wood, textiles and paper, decrease structural strength, and make materials more porous and fragile. Fungi may cause loss of protein or starch sizing in paper. These growths can result in scattered spots known as foxing on paper prints or drawings. A visual examination may locate stains as pigmentations on a surface; mold can appear as velvety growth of almost any color or as a powdery deposit.

sources.title: National Park Service, Conserve O Gram 13/3: Polyester Encapsulation
sources.text:
Polyester encapsulation sandwiches a paper object between two pieces of stiff, chemically inert, clear plastic. All four edges are sealed to hold the paper. It supports and protects fragile or damaged papers. Removing the object requires cutting the encapsulation open; U-seal and L-seal alternatives allow extraction without destroying the enclosure but provide somewhat less protection. It is useful for maps, newspapers and documents needing both sides visible.
Electrostatic charge holds paper fragments in alignment, but damages friable media such as charcoal, pastel, or flaking watercolor; encapsulation should not be used with these objects. Early gelatin photographs should not be kept in polyester folders because the emulsion may stick to plastic or develop shiny ferrotyping spots.
Buffering acidic paper before permanent encapsulation is recommended; a magnesium or calcium carbonate reserve neutralizes existing and future acids. Buffering is an interventive treatment for a paper conservator.

sources.title: National Park Service, Conserve O Gram 13/2: How to Flatten Folded or Rolled Paper Collections
sources.locator: Introduction/cautions lines 24–38; humidification process 66–85; drying cautions 88–111
sources.text:
Many rolled or folded paper materials can be safely relaxed using carefully controlled humidification and then flattened. Papers with iron gall ink and objects in poor condition (large tears, embrittlement) require additional expertise and should only be treated by a professional conservator.
The humidification duration depends on paper weight and type and chamber airtightness. The process uses a chamber, wet muslin, acrylic egg-crate, spun polyester support and periodic checks. Check the paper every 15 minutes in the first hour, then every 30 minutes until relaxed. The process is complete when the object feels damp and pliable and the folds or creases have relaxed.
Humidified paper must be dried as described; air-drying causes curl, warp and distortion. Dry by blotters in a weighted stack and replace damp blotters as directed.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Adjusted Water Washing of a 19th Century American Lithograph
sources.locator: Testing and Washing, lines 32–56; treatment outcomes lines 59–68
sources.text:
Adjusting the bath water with chelators to remove otherwise insoluble metal salts, and buffers to maintain the pH of the bath, can improve the effectiveness of a washing treatment.
Agarose plugs prepared with different washing solutions were applied to various stains to observe which solution most effectively reduced them. The selected blotter-washing solution contained citric acid as a weak chelator and tetrasodium borate as a buffer. Persistent stains were treated with local agarose gel applications, followed by screen washing with deionized water adjusted to pH 7.5 with saturated calcium hydroxide. Treatment aimed to improve image legibility and strengthen weak, brittle paper.

§3.2.1 Work: An abstract entity representing the intellectual or artistic creation. A work is recognized through individual realizations or expressions; revisions, abridgements, and translations generally represent new expressions of the same work.
§3.2.2 Expression: The intellectual or artistic realization of a work in the form of alphanumeric, musical or choreographic notation, sound, image, object, movement, etc. Differences in intellectual or artistic form create a new expression.
§3.2.3 Manifestation: The physical embodiment of an expression of a work. A manifestation represents all the physical objects that bear the same characteristics, both with respect to intellectual content and physical form. Copies resulting from the same production process are part of one manifestation; changes in physical form or medium may create a different manifestation.
§3.2.4 Item: A single exemplar of a manifestation. It is a concrete entity, often a physical object, and can comprise more than one object. Differences that occur after production, such as damage or a library binding variation, distinguish one item from another. The item entity can also reflect unique characteristics such as an autograph or missing notes.
§4.5.3–4.5.6: Item attributes include provenance, marks/inscriptions, and condition, including missing pages, brittleness, or faded images.
